newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rwandan strongman wishes Kabila success in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan strongman wishes Kabila success in Zaire.

text.p: Rwandan Vice-President and military supremo Paul Kagame said he hoped Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila would seize power in Zaire but denied Rwanda was giving him military support.
"I hope the rebels will succeed in their plan because Kabila does the right thing as far as I'm concerned," Major-General Kagame told the Belgian Humo magazine in an interview published on Wednesday.
"It will not be very diplomatic to say this as Vice-President of a neighbouring country, but I don't like the current Zairean rulers," he said.
Kabila's rebels have seized about a quarter of Africa's third largest country since their campaign began last October.
Kagame, who is also Defence Minister, said Zaire's population had taken Kabila's side. "I think he is the stabilising factor, after all that has happened in Zaire in the past years," he said.
Western intelligence sources have said serving members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army are fighting alongside Kabila, but Kagame denied this.
"The Zairean problem is an internal affair. We have no ambition to interfere," he said.

"Satellite pictures which purport to show (that Rwandan troops are operating in Zaire) are circulating, but I don't know of any satellite which can make the distinction between a Rwandan and Zairean black person," he said.
Kagame also said that the endless discussions about whether or not an international force had to be sent to Central Africa were becoming "ridiculous".

But he would not oppose such a force if it only had a humanitarian mission and would not intervene to save the regime of President Mobutu Sese Seko or get between the troops of Kabila and armed Hutus.
Kagame dismissed the need for an African Great Lakes conference aimed at restoring peace in the region.
"Why doesn't the international community understand that a number of Zaireans want to free the country of a corrupt military regime?" he said.

He added that Rwanda's Tutsi-led government wanted to organise free elections in the long term but dismissed suggestions he would have to surrender power to the Hutu majority if elections were to take place.
"You cannot count Hutus and Tutsis like you count cows," he said. "People have to be elected on the basis of their programmes. Hutus and Tutsis have to cooperate in one political party."
He said the Rwandan population hesitated to work for the reconstruction of the country because the government had not yet managed to restore security in the entire country.
"But support increases every day," he said.
